title: Cloud Architecture, Regions & Service Models (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS)
summary: Understand the physical footprint behind cloud Regions and Availability Zones alongside the IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS Shared Responsibility boundaries.
learningObjectives: Differentiate IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS by operational ownership under the Shared Responsibility Model
Architect workloads across Regions and Availability Zones (AZs) to survive data center outages

sections.heading: 1. Physical Cloud Topology & Shared Responsibility Boundaries
sections.content:
Modern cloud platforms are NOT amorphous abstractions—they run on physically isolated data centers grouped into geographically distinct Regions (e.g., us-east-1, ap-south-1). Each Region contains multiple independent Availability Zones (AZs) connected by ultra-low-latency private fiber links while isolating power, cooling, and flood risks.

Meanwhile, the Shared Responsibility Model defines exactly what the provider secures ('Security OF the Cloud': concrete physical security, hypervisors, network racks) vs what your engineering team must configure safely ('Security IN the Cloud': OS kernel patching in IaaS, IAM identities, encryption keys, VPC firewall rules, and application secrets).

codeExamples.explanation: Multi-AZ separation mirrors active application nodes and database replicas across physically separate data centers inside the same region.

keyPoints: Regions protect against regional disasters and satisfy data residency regulations (GDPR, DPDP).
Availability Zones provide fault isolation inside one region with synchronous or near-zero-latency replication.
Under IaaS (EC2/VMs), the customer patches the guest OS; under PaaS/Serverless, the provider patches the runtime.
commonMistakes: Assuming cloud data is automatically distributed across multiple continents by default.
Believing the cloud vendor secures misconfigured S3 buckets or wildcard IAM admin roles.

sections.heading: 2. Selecting Service Models & Infrastructure-as-Code Verification
sections.content: In real engineering environments, teams rarely click settings manually in web consoles because manual clicks cause undocumented configuration drift. Declarative Infrastructure as Code (Terraform / CloudFormation) version-controls every region, subnet, and responsibility boundary cleanly.

codeExamples.explanation: Querying live active Availability Zones programmatically guarantees deployments span multiple isolated power and network domains.

keyPoints: Match workload requirements cleanly: static web apps -> CDN/Object Storage; APIs -> Containers/PaaS; event hooks -> Serverless.
Always track infrastructure changes via pull requests in Git rather than manual console toggles.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding regional AZ availability strings that break when reused in newer accounts or regions.

exercises.title: Responsibility & Service Tier Classification Audit
exercises.objective: Map security and maintenance ownership accurately across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS systems.
exercises.description: A startup deploys three components: an Ubuntu PostgreSQL VM (EC2), a managed serverless webhook function (Lambda), and corporate email (Google Workspace). Classify customer vs provider responsibility for OS patching, data encryption, IAM policies, and physical cooling.
instructions: Identify which layers belong to Customer vs Cloud Provider for the Ubuntu EC2 instance.
Contrast how OS maintenance shifts for the managed serverless function.
Explain why IAM roles and uploaded database secrets remain 100% customer responsibility in ALL three models.
exercises.starterCode:
# Shared Responsibility Matrix
1. Ubuntu EC2 (IaaS):
   - Provider owns: ...
   - Customer owns: ...
2. Serverless Webhook (FaaS/PaaS):
   - Provider owns: ...
   - Customer owns: ...
hints: Hypervisors, concrete walls, and generator fuel belong to the provider in all models.
Customer accounts, access permissions, and application logic always belong to the customer.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: In IaaS, you patch Ubuntu and tune firewalls; in serverless/PaaS, the provider patches runtimes while you own code, IAM, and data safety.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: In the Cloud Shared Responsibility Model for an IaaS virtual machine (e.g., AWS EC2), who is responsible for applying Linux security patches inside the VM?

options.text: Patches are unnecessary in virtual machines

knowledgeChecks.explanation: In IaaS, the customer owns the guest OS, installed packages, firewall Security Groups, and application data.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why do resilient architectures span at least two Availability Zones within a Region?

options.text: To survive a single physical data center power, cooling, or fiber failure with minimal latency
Because single-AZ regions refuse HTTPS TLS certificates
To avoid creating any VPC subnets

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Availability Zones are physically isolated facilities inside a region designed for fault containment.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which service model lets developers push pure function handlers triggered by HTTP/events without managing servers or OS upgrades?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Serverless Function-as-a-Service automates server provisioning, scaling, and runtime OS patching.

recap: You mastered physical Regions vs AZ isolation and clear ownership split across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS under the Shared Responsibility Model.
